doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Accompanying Jimmy Rushing and Big Maybelle in Ohio and Buffalo
summary: Jeannie played for visiting singers as the house band in Ohio and Buffalo, with stories of Jimmy Rushing teaching her a song and Big Maybelle working the crowd.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Well let me catch up on a couple of things in your history here. When did you first have a chance to accompany some of those singers — Dinah Washington and —

Actually, that was all through the 50s, most of it. Big Maybelle and Jimmy Witherspoon and Dinah Washington and Mr. Five by Five — Jimmy Rushing, who came. And I had never played [sings] “I want a little girl to call my own.”

No. Jimmy Rushing. But none of them had music. They never had any music. And I was used to reading everything see? So I said, “Well I don’t know that song.” He said, “It goes like this,” and he sits down to play more piano than most piano players. A very excellent pianist. Show me the bridge [scats] — whooo, okay. But he was very nice. And I played with Big Mama Thornton and they were all—

And Joe Williams, and Wynonie Harris. And it was lucky because it was all in that same area like Columbus, Springfield and Dayton. Because we were like the house band in Ohio. Cleveland Ohio. And some of it was in Buffalo, New York where they had this club where I played for Big Maybelle. You’ve heard of Big Maybelle?

Big Maybelle was — I had a day off and I had gone to bed and the bass player, his name was Shakespeare, we called him Shakespeare because he could read his own palm. And he came knocking on the door “Jeannie! Jeannie! Get up. There’s a woman down here made me give her all my money.” I knew, he was so tight, he would tell us, “I’m not buying any Christmas gifts so don’t buy me anything.” That’s how tight he was. So I © Fillius Jazz Archive -26-

knew if she made him give her all his money, I knew that something was really up. So I got dressed really fast and we went down and there were limousines all around this club. We could hardly push our way in. And here was this lady with this baby face. She weighed almost 350 pounds, and she was going through the aisle singing [sings] “Baby please don’t go.” And as she walked she had these pockets, and people were stuffing hundred dollar bills in. And she was still singing. She would hit that hip and make that money go around in there and keep moving, but tears was coming down her cheeks singing this song. And I never heard or saw anything like that. This was an inter-racial audience. It was full of people with limousines who had come from miles around to watch this woman sing. She could really, really work a crowd. And she could make me cry. And she’d sing songs — you know I’ll tell what was wonderful about people like her. And Joe Williams, a lot of them, they all sang not just blues, not just rhythm and blues, they’d sing songs like [sings] “If God made me a king/I’d be but a fool for you.” They’d sing all those beautiful ballads.
